title: Query optimisation: plan space
lead: Parsing, rewriting, algebraic equivalences, pushdown and physical alternatives.

sections.title: Query optimisation and query lifecycle
sections.html:
The optimiser seeks a correct execution plan with low estimated cost. It searches a restricted candidate space rather than guaranteeing the globally fastest program. The parser checks syntax, schemas and permissions, then constructs query blocks.

The rewriter applies semantic simplifications and algebraic equivalences. It can remove impossible or redundant predicates when the schema justifies doing so. The cost-based optimiser enumerates alternatives, estimates their costs using catalog statistics and selects a plan for execution.

This PDF has four printed slides per physical page. Page references here identify the physical PDF page; printed slide numbers are separate.

PDF pp. 1–2

sections.title: Plan space and algebraic equivalences
sections.html:
Optimisation has three concerns: the candidate plan space, the cost model and the search algorithm. Plan-space rules determine which relational expressions may replace one another without changing results.

Selections can be split and reordered. Projections can move earlier only if they preserve every attribute needed later. Inner joins can be reordered with their predicates, but an intermediate pair without a connecting condition is a Cartesian product. Outer joins and SQL NULL or duplicate semantics require additional care.

Changing a join tree is therefore more than swapping names in a diagram: predicates, output attributes and multiplicities must remain correct.

PDF pp. 3–4

sections.title: Selection and projection pushdown
sections.html:
Selection pushdown applies a predicate as soon as its referenced attributes are available. It usually reduces the rows processed by later operators. Transitive equalities can expose additional legal joins, such as deriving R.A = T.C from R.A = S.B and S.B = T.C.

Projection pushdown removes attributes that no later predicate, join, grouping or output expression requires. Narrower tuples reduce intermediate storage and can change how much data fits in memory.

Avoiding unnecessary Cartesian products is another heuristic. These rules expose promising plans without requiring precise cost estimates, but their I/O effect depends on access methods, repeated scans and materialisation.

PDF pp. 5–6

sections.title: Physical plan alternatives
sections.html:
A logical operator can have several physical implementations. Base-table access may use a heap scan or an applicable index. An equijoin may use block nested loops, index nested loops, sort-merge or hash join.

Each implementation has prerequisites and properties: index probes require a matching index, sort-merge requires suitable ordering or sorting, and hash join requires equality keys and memory management. General non-equality predicates can use nested loops.

The plan space combines access methods, join order and operator implementations. Subsequent lectures estimate the cost of these combinations and describe how to search them efficiently.

PDF pp. 7

quiz.question: Which columns must projection pushdown retain?
options: Only the columns in the final SELECT list
Output columns and every column still needed by later operators
quiz.explanation: Join keys and filter columns remain necessary even when they are absent from the final SELECT list.

Coverage includes the parser, rewriter, and cost-based optimizer; query blocks and the System R approach; logical equivalences and safe simplifications; join reordering, cross products, and transitive predicates; selection and projection pushdown; and physical implementation choices. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
